BUDAPEST, Hungary: Hungary's former nationalist prime minister Viktor Orbán, who lost power after 16 years in an election in April, has called on his supporters to restore democracy. He said that the new government has destroyed democracy in the country. Orbán made his first strong political comments since his heavy election defeat late on July 21 through a Facebook post. He issued what he called a "Statement of Resistance" shortly after his Fidesz party said that prosecutors had searched offices where its internet servers are located. Prosecutors told Reuters in an email that the action was connected to an investigation into suspected misuse of funds and other crimes at the National Culture Fund (NKA) during Orbán's time in government. Orbán said that Hungary is no longer a democratic state after the new center-right government led by Prime Minister Peter Magyar passed a constitutional amendment. According to Orbán, this amendment ended the terms of both the president and the head of the constitutional court. Magyar's Tisza party has denied accusations that it is acting in an authoritarian way toward political opponents. The party has promised to reduce corruption, which it says was widespread under Orbán's government, as part of its effort to bring Hungary back in line with the European Union. Orbán himself faced strong criticism during his time in power over democratic standards in Hungary. His government often clashed with the European Union on issues such as the rule of law and the rights of minorities. Orbán has denied all corruption allegations. He said that a period of tyranny had begun again in Hungary. He also said that the new political system created in this way is not legitimate, and that Fidesz will use all peaceful means, both inside and outside parliament, to oppose what he described as abuse of power. Magyar's Tisza party holds a large majority in parliament, which allows it to reverse changes introduced during Orbán's time in office that Magyar says weakened democracy. The constitutional amendment ended the term of President Tamás Sulyok, stating that there had been a serious loss of public trust in him. Sulyok had been elected in 2024 by lawmakers from Orbán's Fidesz party. Parliament is expected to elect a new president soon. Magyar's Tisza party currently enjoys strong public support. A poll by the polling company Median earlier in the month showed that 60 percent of voters support Tisza, compared to 18 percent for Fidesz. Since the election, Fidesz has faced internal problems, including the resignation of its parliamentary group leader last week. Photograph: Jae C Hong/AP California Six Flags permanently shuts down X2 rollercoaster after claims of brain injuries More than 100 people have said they were injured by the ride in California, which reaches up to 76mph Uwa Ede-Osifo Tue 29 Sep 2026 16.16 EDT Last modified on Tue 29 Sep 2026 16.17 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Six Flags has permanently shut down its embattled X2 rollercoaster in Valencia, California , the company announced on Tuesday, as a groundswell of past riders have come forward with allegations of serious injuries. X2, a Magic Mountain park favorite, which reaches up to 76mph (about 122km/h) and has seats that can rotate 360 degrees, had been closed since mid-July. In August , a CNN investigation revealed two riders had suffered brain hemorrhages in July. One of the two, Los Angeles resident Naomi Greer-Wilkinson, remains hospitalized in a semi-conscious state, according to her lawyers Gary Dordick and Christopher Bulone. CNN also found at least two deaths allegedly linked to X2. The scope of X2’s alleged harm has ballooned after the network’s reporting. More than 100 people have said they were injured by the ride according to Bulone and Dordick, who filed three new civil lawsuits against the amusement park. The attorneys have called X2 “defective” and accused the amusement park of failing to adequately warn riders of the risk for head and brain injuries, according to court documents. Brian Oerding, the Magic Mountain park president, alluded to the public controversy while announcing X2’s closure. “While X2 consistently passed a multitude of safety tests, we have decided to close the ride because we believe it’s the right thing to do. Ride safety is a cornerstone of our business, and when we see guest confidence affected, we take it seriously,” he wrote in a Tuesday blog post. “Since X2 opened in 2008, it has welcomed more than 16 million guests and earned a passionate following among ride enthusiasts. We recognize the special place X2 holds in the coaster community, and we are grateful to our team members who operated and maintained it throughout its run.” Explore more on these topics California Los Angeles West Coast news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness

https://www.fox17online.com/news/local-n.text: Grand Rapids is preparing for its 54th annual Pulaski Days celebration, a week-long event honoring Polish heritage taking place throughout October at 13 participating Polish halls and organizations across the city.The celebration brings together families, friends, neighbors, and visitors from across West Michigan for food, live music, dancing, fellowship, and cultural traditions. Each of the 13 Polish clubs and fraternal organizations opens its doors to the public, offering its own unique way to mark the occasion.CHECK OUT THE LINK TO PULASKI DAYS FULL SCHEDULE HEREThis year's theme is "Rooted in Pride, United Inside."What began as a weekend celebration in 1972 to support and promote Grand Rapids' Polish halls has grown into a week-long community tradition.
